findings.title: Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently discards the original method
findings.body: Two `def self.downsize` methods are now defined (lines 145-147 and 149-151) with different arities: `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby, the second definition overwrites the first at load time (Ruby emits a 'method redefined' warning), so the original 4-argument signature becomes permanently unreachable. Any existing caller elsewhere in the codebase that calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height, opts)` with four positional arguments will now raise an ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments) or silently misinterpret `height` as part of the options hash. This is dead/conflicting code that should be removed/merged rather than left as two definitions.

findings.title: Percentage dimension string is invalid for gifsicle-based animated downsizing
findings.body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` passes a percentage string as the resize dimension. When `allow_animation` is true and the file is a GIF, this routes to `downsize_instructions_animated` → `resize_instructions_animated`, which runs `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. Gifsicle's `--resize-fit`/`--resize` options require an explicit `WxH` pair and do not accept percentage syntax, so the command will fail. Consequence: animated GIFs larger than `max_image_size_kb` will never actually be downsized (the shell command errors out every iteration), the while loop will exhaust all 5 attempts without reducing the file, and the oversized/animated original will still be uploaded, defeating the stated purpose of the feature for this file type.

findings.title: Downsizing an oversized animated GIF can permanently strip its animation
findings.body: When `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is false (the typical default), the downsizing call falls back to `downsize_instructions`, whose ImageMagick command reads `#{from}[0]` — i.e. only the first frame of the source. Because this logic is now applied directly to the user's original uploaded file (not just to a generated thumbnail), any animated GIF that exceeds `max_image_size_kb` will be silently converted into a static single-frame image before it is ever stored. This is a destructive, user-visible content change with no warning, caused purely by reusing thumbnail-oriented resize instructions on the original upload.

findings.title: In-place resize uses the same path for input and output
findings.body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` uses the identical path for both the source and destination of the external `convert`/`gifsicle` command. Tools that open the output file for writing (truncating it) before fully reading/processing the input (gifsicle in particular, via `--output`) risk truncating or corrupting the source file before processing completes, resulting in a zero-byte or corrupted temp file being uploaded. A safer pattern is to write to a distinct temporary path and then replace the original once the conversion succeeds.

findings.title: No handling for failed downsize attempts or files still over the limit after 5 tries
findings.body: The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` and decrements `attempt`, but never checks the boolean return value of `downsize` (which is false on shell-command failure) nor reports anything if, after 5 attempts, the file is still larger than `max_image_size_kb`. In both cases (repeated failures, or diminishing returns from 80% scaling not reaching the target), the code proceeds to call `Upload.create_for` with a file that may still exceed the configured size limit or may be corrupted, with no user-facing error or log entry indicating the size restriction was not honored.

findings.title: Hardcoded 10MB cap replaces configurable max_image_size_kb for URL-based uploads
findings.body: The API URL download limit changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. This removes admin configurability: sites that configure `max_image_size_kb` smaller than 10MB will now allow larger downloads than intended before any downsizing occurs, and sites that configure it larger than 10MB can no longer fetch URLs beyond 10MB even though their own size policy would otherwise permit it. This also applies uniformly regardless of upload `type` (image vs. attachment), losing any type-specific limit that existed before.

findings.title: Client-side upload size validation no longer respects per-type site settings
findings.body: `maxSizeKB` in `validateUploadedFile` was changed from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` to a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. This removes the distinction between image and attachment size limits and ignores whatever the admin has actually configured (e.g. `max_image_size_kb`, `max_attachment_size_kb`). As a result, client-side validation can now accept files that the server would reject (if the configured limit is lower than 10MB) or reject files the server would accept (if the configured limit is higher), and the error message shown to users will state an incorrect maximum size relative to the server's actual configuration.

findings.title: 413 error message now shows a hardcoded size instead of the configured max_image_size_kb
findings.body: In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 (entity too large) handler replaced `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. If the site's actual configured `max_image_size_kb` (or webserver/proxy upload limit) differs from 10MB, the error message presented to the user will state the wrong maximum allowed size, which is misleading and inconsistent with the rest of the validation logic.

findings.title: No tests added for new image auto-downsizing behavior
findings.body: This PR introduces non-trivial new logic (a bounded retry loop invoking external image-processing commands on the original uploaded file, with different code paths for animated vs. static images) but includes no new or updated specs covering it. Given the identified risks (gifsicle percentage argument failure, animation stripped from GIFs, in-place file corruption potential, and the changed `OptimizedImage.downsize` method signature), the lack of test coverage leaves these regressions and edge cases unverified before merge.
